name: Ectoparasite Infestations and Arthropod Injuries
system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)

clinicalPearls: Of all organisms in this chapter, only the human itch mite (Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis) and human-infesting lice are obligate human parasites; humans are accidental or dead-end hosts for most others.

Scabies affects roughly 250 million people worldwide and is spread mainly by direct skin-to-skin contact; transmission via shared bedding or clothing is less common than widely assumed, and mites usually die within about a day off a suitable host.

Scabies pruritus reflects a sensitization reaction; an initial infestation can stay asymptomatic for up to about 6 weeks, but reinfestation provokes prompt hypersensitivity. Itch typically worsens at night and after hot showers.

Crusted (formerly Norwegian) scabies arises in glucocorticoid use, immunodeficiency (including HIV/AIDS), and neuropsychiatric conditions that blunt itching/scratching; it harbors thousands of mites, is highly contagious, often non-pruritic, lacks classic burrows, and can mimic psoriasis.

Confirmation of louse infestation should rest on finding a live louse, not on nits alone, since hatched/dead eggs (and pseudo-nits of debris/dander/fungi) remain cemented to hair for months and are frequently misread as active disease.

Body lice (not head lice) are the recognized vectors of epidemic (louse-borne) typhus, louse-borne relapsing fever, and trench fever; outbreaks track societal upheaval, crowding, and inability to launder clothing.

Furuncular myiasis (e.g., Dermatobia hominis, Cordylobia anthropophaga) presents as a boil-like nodule with a central breathing pore that emits bubbles when submerged in water, and the patient may sense movement within the skin.

Brown recluse (Loxosceles) envenomation classically produces a painful lesion with central induration, a pale ischemic zone, and surrounding erythema, sometimes evolving to a necrotic black eschar; widow spider (Latrodectus) bites cause minimal local injury but severe neurotoxic muscle cramps via alpha-latrotoxin.
Removing hard ticks within the first 24 hours of attachment generally prevents transmission of Lyme disease, babesiosis, anaplasmosis, and ehrlichiosis, though tick-borne viruses may transmit faster.

Tick paralysis is an acute ascending flaccid Guillain-Barre-like paralysis from a salivary toxin; sensory exam and lumbar puncture are typically normal, and finding/removing the hidden tick (often under scalp hair) reverses it within hours.

Alpha-gal syndrome (red-meat allergy) follows tick bites that induce IgE against galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose, a carbohydrate present in non-primate mammalian muscle; in the US it is linked to the lone star tick.
Most reported 'spider bites' are not spider-related; acute tender noduloulcerative lesions are frequently due to minor trauma or bacterial infection, particularly MRSA.
harrison.pathophysiology: Ectoparasites are arthropods and organisms of other phyla that infest skin or hair; they may remain superficial (anchored by mouthparts or claws) or penetrate into epidermis, dermis, or subcutaneous tissue. Injury arises through several mechanisms: direct mechanical damage, consumption of blood or nutrients, hypersensitivity reactions to saliva/secretions/excretions, inoculation of toxins or venoms, transmission of pathogens, and creation of skin portals for secondary bacterial infection. In scabies, gravid female mites burrow within the stratum corneum and lay eggs; rash and pruritus result from delayed-type sensitization, with burrows surrounded by infiltrates of eosinophils, lymphocytes, and histiocytes. Lice are obligate blood feeders whose saliva produces a pruritic morbilliform/urticarial reaction in sensitized hosts. Venom-mediated injury is prominent in arachnid and hymenopteran envenomation: widow spider alpha-latrotoxin binds irreversibly to presynaptic terminals causing release then depletion of acetylcholine and norepinephrine; bark scorpion neurotoxins hold sodium channels open producing cranial-nerve and neuromuscular hyperexcitability; some scorpion venoms trigger massive catecholamine release with cardiopulmonary toxicity. Hymenopteran venoms contain amines, kinins, and enzymes (e.g., melittin, phospholipases, hyaluronidase) producing local and systemic effects, with most fatalities due to IgE-mediated type 1 anaphylaxis. Tick salivary secretions are biologically active anticoagulants that can transmit pathogens and provoke sterile inflammatory responses, fever, and toxin-mediated paralysis.
additionalDifferentials: Papular urticaria from other arthropod bites
Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis (purpuric papules resembling chigger bites)
Cutaneous larva migrans (resembling serpiginous migratory fly-larva eruptions)
Bacterial cellulitis (mimicked by large local hymenopteran sting reactions)
Peritonitis / acute surgical abdomen (mimicked by widow spider envenomation abdominal rigidity)
infectionMimics: MRSA and other bacterial skin infections misattributed to spider bites
Impetigo / cellulitis as secondary infection of scabies or louse excoriations
Bacterial cellulitis confused with large local Hymenoptera sting reactions
nonInfectiousMimics: Delusional infestation (Ekbom syndrome / delusory parasitosis), with self-induced excoriations and ulcers and no true parasite
Pseudo-nits (debris, dry skin flakes, hair fungi) mistaken for louse eggs
additionalInvestigations: Microscopic examination of skin scrapings from unroofed burrows for mites, eggs, and fecal pellets (scabies)
Skin biopsy, cellophane-tape or cyanoacrylate adhesive lift, and dermatoscopy of papulovesicular lesions
Direct identification of the offending arthropod from a collected specimen (taken from patient, traps, or environment) with proper fixation/preservation for taxonomic review
Examination of clothing seams for body lice and nits; inspection of hair for live lice
Skin tests and venom-specific RAST for Hymenoptera hypersensitivity to guide immunotherapy
PCR of captured lice has detected pathogenic bacteria in research settings
redFlags: Ascending flaccid paralysis with cranial-nerve involvement after tick attachment (tick paralysis) progressing to respiratory failure if the tick is not found and removed
Rapid anaphylaxis after Hymenoptera or reduviid bite (upper-airway edema, bronchospasm, hypotension, shock) usually beginning within 10 minutes
Stings to the tongue or mouth causing life-threatening upper-airway edema
Scorpion envenomation with cranial-nerve dysfunction, neuromuscular hyperexcitability, hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia, pulmonary edema, or rhabdomyolysis
Widow spider envenomation with severe muscle cramping, respiratory distress, hypertension, or premature labor
Recluse spider envenomation with systemic hemolysis, renal failure, or expanding necrosis
Lonomia obliqua caterpillar contact causing disseminated coagulopathy and hemorrhagic shock
Halzoun/marrara (Linguatula serrata pentastomiasis) with severe pharyngeal edema requiring tracheostomy
Aeromonas hydrophila sepsis, myonecrosis, or intractable bleeding complicating medicinal leech therapy
harrison.prognosis: Most infestations and bites are self-limited or readily treated. Scabies becomes noncommunicable within about a day of proper treatment, though hypersensitivity pruritus may persist for weeks as dead mites and debris are cleared; secondary streptococcal infection can lead to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and possibly acute rheumatic fever. Brown recluse lesions usually heal within about 3 months, and verified deaths from North American brown recluse bites have not been confirmed. Widow spider pain typically begins subsiding within the first 12 hours but may recur over days to weeks; fatal outcomes are rare and concentrated in the very young, elderly, or debilitated. Bark scorpion envenomation peaks around 5 hours and subsides over a day or two, with fatal respiratory arrest mainly in young children and the elderly. Tick paralysis generally resolves within hours to days after tick removal but can be fatal from respiratory paralysis or aspiration if untreated. Hymenoptera-related deaths (>=100/year in the US) result almost entirely from anaphylaxis.
pitfalls: Diagnosing scabies or an 'outbreak' without confirmation; unrelated skin diseases are frequently misdiagnosed as scabies.
Treating residual nits as active louse infestation; onerous 'no-nit' school exclusion policies are increasingly viewed as unjustified and counterproductive.
Over-treating with topical scabicides/pediculicides, which can cause irritant contact dermatitis (especially repeated permethrin).
Treating environmental (non-burrowing) mites such as chiggers with acaricides on the patient, which is discouraged because these mites do not reside on humans.
Attributing necrotic skin lesions to spider bites without observation of a spider; many are bacterial (often MRSA) or traumatic.
Delaying tick removal by applying heat or occlusive substances, which merely prolongs attachment; ticks should be removed by traction with fine-tipped forceps at the mouthparts.
Mistaking widow spider abdominal rigidity for a surgical abdomen and performing unnecessary surgery (the abdomen is not tender on palpation).
Interpreting childhood eyelash (pubic louse) infestation as incontrovertible proof of sexual abuse.
Failing to recognize delusional infestation, leading to repeated futile antiparasitic treatment.
harrison.severityClassification: No formal numeric staging is given; severity is graded clinically by host reaction and systemic involvement. Scabies ranges from ordinary (typically <=10-15 burrows) to crusted/hyperinfested (thousands of mites, highly contagious). Arthropod envenomations are stratified from local-only reactions (most scorpion and spider bites: pain, edema) to systemic/life-threatening envenomation (cranial-nerve and neuromuscular dysfunction, cardiopulmonary toxicity, hemolysis, renal failure). Hymenoptera reactions span uncomplicated local stings, large local hypersensitivity reactions spreading >=10 cm over 1-2 days, and systemic type 1 anaphylaxis.
management: Treat scabies with topical permethrin or oral ivermectin, applied correctly and repeated to cover the mite life cycle, and treat all close contacts simultaneously
Manage crusted scabies with combined oral ivermectin and a topical scabicide plus keratolytics, under barrier isolation given the enormous mite burden
Treat louse infestation with a topical pediculicide such as permethrin or dimeticone or with oral therapy, confirming live lice, and for body lice launder or heat-treat clothing and improve hygiene
Relieve pruritus and hypersensitivity with antihistamines and topical corticosteroids, and treat secondary bacterial infection with antibacterials
Provide wound care and careful tick or stinger removal for bites and stings, and treat systemic envenomation and anaphylaxis with adrenaline and supportive care
Refer patients with systemic allergic reactions for Hymenoptera venom immunotherapy

Decontaminate the environment and treat household or institutional contacts to prevent reinfestation, and watch for louse-borne systemic infection such as typhus, relapsing fever and trench fever in at-risk settings
